title: Professional Responsibility: Conflict of Interest & Confidentiality
prompt: You are an associate at a small firm. A long-standing business client, Acme LLC, asks the firm to draft an operating agreement for a new venture Acme is forming with a second person, Blair. Blair is also an individual client of yours — you drafted Blair's will last year — and Blair separately mentions to you, in confidence, that Blair is worried Acme is 'over-promising' and privately intends to keep an exit option Acme doesn't know about. Acme now wants you to represent 'the deal' and draft terms favorable to getting it done. Walk me through the professional-responsibility issues and how you would handle this. This is a spoken discussion.
blurb: A professional-responsibility roleplay — spot the concurrent conflict and the confidentiality trap, apply the Model Rules, and reason to a defensible course of action.

rubric.label: Issue spotting
rubric.description: Identifies the concurrent conflict of interest between two current clients (Acme and Blair) whose interests in the venture are directly adverse or materially limited, AND the separate confidentiality problem created by Blair's private disclosure. Recognizes the joint-representation dimension.

rubric.label: Command of the rules
rubric.description: Correctly invokes the governing standards: Model Rule 1.7 (concurrent conflicts, informed consent confirmed in writing, non-consentable conflicts), 1.6 (confidentiality), 1.9 (duties to former clients if applicable), 1.4 (communication), and the 'reasonable lawyer' consentability limit.

rubric.label: Analysis & application
rubric.description: Applies the rules to facts: whether the conflict is consentable, why Blair's secret exit intent makes joint representation untenable (the lawyer cannot use or reveal it to Acme yet cannot keep it from a client it jointly represents), and the informed-consent/waiver mechanics.

rubric.label: Confidentiality reasoning
rubric.description: Reasons carefully about Rule 1.6: the lawyer may not disclose Blair's confidence to Acme, but also cannot draft against Blair's undisclosed interest or mislead Acme; recognizes the 'no secrets' premise of joint representation and the resulting impasse.

rubric.label: Sound course of action
rubric.description: Reaches a defensible resolution: decline the joint 'represent the deal' engagement or obtain informed written consent only if permissible; more likely advise both to seek separate counsel; do not proceed in a way that harms either client or misuses confidences. Avoids just 'getting the deal done.'

rubric.label: Professional judgment
rubric.description: Prioritizes duties to clients over the firm's business interest in the fee, documents consents, and considers screening/withdrawal where required; shows candor.

rubric.label: Communication & clarity
rubric.description: Explains the issues clearly and in an organized way, distinguishing the conflict question from the confidentiality question rather than blurring them.

reference.scenario: A concurrent conflict of interest layered on top of a confidentiality trap. The firm currently represents both Acme and Blair (Blair is a current client from the will matter, or at minimum a former client whose confidences persist). Acme and Blair are forming a venture and their interests are potentially adverse; Acme's request to draft terms 'favorable to getting it done' and Blair's secret intent to keep an undisclosed exit option make the adversity concrete. Under Model Rule 1.7, this is a concurrent conflict: representing one client will be directly adverse to, or materially limited by duties to, the other. A 1.7 conflict is consentable only if the lawyer reasonably believes she can competently and diligently represent both, it is not prohibited by law, the clients are not asserting claims against each other in the same proceeding, and each gives informed consent confirmed in writing. The confidentiality wrinkle is decisive: Blair disclosed, in confidence, an intent adverse to the very deal. Under Rule 1.6 the lawyer cannot reveal that to Acme; but joint representation runs on a 'no secrets among jointly represented clients' premise, and the lawyer cannot draft a deal for Acme while sitting on Blair's material, adverse secret — that makes the conflict effectively non-consentable here, because the lawyer cannot provide competent, diligent, candid representation to Acme without using or revealing Blair's confidence. The sound resolution: the lawyer should not accept the joint 'represent the deal' engagement on these facts; she should decline or limit the engagement, keep Blair's confidence, avoid drafting against either client, and advise the parties to obtain separate counsel — and consider whether she must withdraw from or wall off aspects of the existing relationships. She must not prioritize the fee or 'getting the deal done.' A weak candidate blesses the joint representation with a boilerplate waiver, ignores the confidentiality impasse, or suggests quietly using or revealing Blair's secret.
model_points: Frame two distinct issues: (1) a concurrent conflict of interest under Rule 1.7, and (2) a confidentiality duty to Blair under Rule 1.6 — do not blur them.

Establish client status: Acme is a current client; Blair is a current client (or a former client under Rule 1.9 whose confidences still bind). Either way the firm owes Blair confidentiality and loyalty duties.

Rule 1.7(a): a concurrent conflict exists — representation of Acme is directly adverse to Blair and/or materially limited by the lawyer's duties to Blair, especially given Blair's undisclosed adverse intent.

Rule 1.7(b) consentability test: allowed only if (i) the lawyer reasonably believes she can provide competent and diligent representation to each, (ii) not prohibited by law, (iii) no assertion of claims by one client against the other in the same litigation, and (iv) each affected client gives informed consent, confirmed in writing.
Informed consent requires full disclosure of the risks — but here the lawyer cannot fully inform Acme without revealing Blair's confidence, which Rule 1.6 forbids. That is the trap.
Rule 1.6: the lawyer must not reveal Blair's confidential exit intent to Acme, and generally may not use it to Blair's disadvantage either.

Joint-representation 'no secrets' premise: a lawyer jointly representing parties ordinarily cannot keep one client's material secret from the other; combined with 1.6, this makes competent joint representation impossible here — the conflict is effectively non-consentable.
Rule 1.4 (communication): the lawyer cannot mislead Acme or draft terms that Acme would not agree to if it knew what the lawyer knows.

Resolution: decline the joint 'represent the deal' engagement; do NOT draft favorable-to-Acme terms while holding Blair's secret; advise both parties to retain separate, independent counsel for the venture.
Handle the existing relationships: keep Blair's confidence, avoid any use of it, and consider whether continued representation of either on this matter requires withdrawal (Rule 1.16) or screening.
Do not let the firm's interest in the fee or 'getting the deal done' override the duties of loyalty and confidentiality.
Document everything: the conflict analysis, any declination, and advice to seek separate counsel.

probes.trigger: candidate says 'just get a conflict waiver and proceed'
probes.question: Walk me through the informed-consent disclosure you'd give Acme. Can you actually make full disclosure without revealing what Blair told you in confidence?

probes.trigger: candidate suggests telling Acme about Blair's secret exit plan
probes.question: You'd disclose Blair's confidence to Acme? What does Rule 1.6 say about that, and where does the authority to reveal come from here?

probes.trigger: candidate proceeds and just drafts neutral terms
probes.question: You know Blair intends an undisclosed exit that Acme would care about. Can you draft this deal for Acme in good conscience while sitting on that? What rule governs?

probes.trigger: candidate treats it purely as a confidentiality issue and misses the conflict
probes.question: Set the secret aside for a second — is there a conflict-of-interest problem just from representing both sides of this venture? Which rule?

probes.trigger: candidate treats it purely as a conflict and misses confidentiality
probes.question: Even if you got written consents, does Blair's private disclosure create a separate problem that consent doesn't solve?

probes.trigger: candidate prioritizes the client relationship or the fee
probes.question: Acme is a major client and this is a nice fee. How much weight does that get in your analysis, and why?

red_flags: Blesses the joint representation with a boilerplate waiver, ignoring that the conflict is effectively non-consentable here.
Proposes revealing Blair's confidence to Acme, violating Rule 1.6.
Proposes secretly using Blair's confidence to Blair's disadvantage while drafting for Acme.
Misses the concurrent-conflict issue and treats it only as confidentiality (or vice versa).
Prioritizes the firm's fee or the client relationship over loyalty/confidentiality duties.
Cannot name or misstates the governing rules (1.7, 1.6, 1.9, 1.4, 1.16).
Thinks informed consent can be given without full disclosure of material risks.
Fails to advise separate counsel or to consider withdrawal/screening.
Cavalier about documentation and about the 'no secrets' premise of joint representation.
follow_ups: Suppose Blair had NOT disclosed the secret exit intent, and the parties genuinely had aligned interests. Could you take the joint engagement then, and on what conditions?
Assume you already started drafting before Blair told you the secret. What are your obligations now — withdraw, and if so, from representing whom?
Does it matter whether Blair is characterized as a current client versus a former client under Rule 1.9? How does the analysis shift?
Could an ethical screen within the firm cure this, with a different lawyer handling Acme? Why or why not?
If Blair's secret involved an intent to defraud Acme, would any exception to Rule 1.6 permit or require disclosure?
reference.exemplar_answer: 'There are two separate problems here, and I want to keep them apart. First, a conflict of interest: we represent Acme, and we also represent Blair — I drafted Blair's will, so Blair is a current client, and even as a former client Blair's confidences bind us. Acme and Blair are on opposite sides of this venture, and Acme wants terms favorable to itself, so under Model Rule 1.7 representing 'the deal' is a concurrent conflict — directly adverse and, at a minimum, materially limited by our duties to Blair. A 1.7 conflict is sometimes consentable: if I reasonably believe I can competently and diligently represent both, it's not prohibited by law, they're not suing each other, and each gives informed consent confirmed in writing. Second, and this is what makes consent impossible here: Blair told me in confidence about an undisclosed intent to keep an exit option Acme doesn't know about. Under Rule 1.6 I cannot reveal that to Acme, and I can't use it against Blair either. But joint representation runs on a no-secrets premise, and to get Acme's truly informed consent I'd have to disclose the very risk I'm forbidden to reveal. I also can't, under Rule 1.4, draft a deal for Acme while withholding something material I know Acme would care about. So the conflict is effectively non-consentable on these facts. My course of action: I would not accept the engagement to represent the deal, and I would not draft Acme-favorable terms while holding Blair's confidence. I'd keep Blair's confidence, decline to use it, and advise both Acme and Blair to retain separate, independent counsel for the venture. I'd also assess whether I need to withdraw from any related matter under Rule 1.16, and I'd document the conflict analysis and my advice. The fact that Acme is a valued client and this is a good fee doesn't change any of that — loyalty and confidentiality come first. The only version where I could proceed is a counterfactual with no secret and genuinely aligned interests, and even then only with full disclosure and written informed consent from both.'

interviewer_notes: Conversational professional-responsibility roleplay. The AI plays a senior partner (or examiner) walking the associate through the scenario and applying pressure toward the 'wrong' answer — Acme is a big client, the fee is attractive, 'can't we just paper it with a waiver?' The two must-spot issues are (1) the Rule 1.7 concurrent conflict and (2) the Rule 1.6 confidentiality trap created by Blair's secret; a strong candidate keeps them distinct and shows WHY the confidentiality problem renders the conflict effectively non-consentable (you cannot give Acme informed consent without revealing what you're forbidden to reveal). Deploy the 'just get a waiver' and 'tell Acme the secret' probes to test whether the candidate protects confidences and understands the limits of consent. The two worst failures are proposing to reveal Blair's confidence (a 1.6 violation) and blessing the joint representation with boilerplate. Reward candidates who name the specific Model Rules, advise separate counsel, consider withdrawal/screening, and refuse to let the fee drive the analysis. Difficulty is mid: expect solid rule command but not necessarily nuances like the 1.6(b) crime-fraud exception — save that for the last follow-up to see how far a strong candidate can go.
